title: National Bureau of Statistics of China, industrial enterprise profits for January to August 2026, published 28 September 2026
snippet: Read in full. The primary source and the only one that carries the figures this article rests on: total profit of 52719.8 hundred million yuan, up 15.7 per cent over the eight months; August alone up 4.2 per cent; operating revenue of 930851.2 hundred million yuan, up 6.6 per cent; operating revenue profit margin of 5.66 per cent, up 0.44 percentage points; receivables collection period of 72.2 days, up 0.9 days; finished-goods inventory turnover of 21.3 days, up 0.6 days; and the industry table, from electronic equipment up 1.1 times over to ferrous metal smelting and rolling down 62.4 per cent. It contains no per-unit or per-container cost table and no working-capital calculation.

title: State Council of China, chart release on the same figures, sourced to Xinhua, 28 September 2026
snippet: Read in full, and it is a chart reproduction rather than new analysis. It corroborates the headline only: 52719.8 hundred million yuan of industrial profit in the first eight months, up 15.7 per cent. No working-capital figures and no cost calculation.

title: Coface APAC Payment Survey 2026, 16th edition, 522 respondents in mainland China, published 14 August 2026
snippet: Read in full. A credit insurer's survey rather than an official release, and it is the corroborating source on the payment behaviour: average payment term offered of 81 days, eleven days above the APAC average; 86 per cent of firms experiencing late payment; average delay of 73 days; 35 per cent reporting more frequent delays against 26 per cent reporting improvement. It also cites the official June 2026 reading of 71.7 days against 70.9 a year earlier, with receivables up 8.1 per cent, which is what establishes the direction independently of the August figure. No per-unit cost table.

title: A quantitative essay on the 15 per cent industrial profit figure and sector divergence
snippet: Read in part. An independent analyst's note that makes the sector-divergence point, framing the headline as a Simpson's paradox in which the aggregate moves one way while the components move differently. It reaches the same observation about composition that this article's industry table supports, but from equity-market data rather than the statistics release, and it contains no working-capital calculation and no per-unit cost figure. Recorded as a competitor on the sector-divergence observation and not on the cash calculation.
